react_vs_plan_and_execute: The measured ReAct workflow uses 5 model calls and 1077 estimated tokens for S1, 3 calls/445 tokens for the cancelled order S5, and 2 calls/144 tokens for NOT_FOUND S6. Each new call resends accumulated history, so its token cost grows with the number and size of observations. A plan-and-execute design could request the full conditional step list once, then execute validated tools locally and replan only on an error; a normal request could use one planning call plus an optional final response call. Its exact token saving is unmeasured because the supplied mock implements ReAct, not a planner. ReAct adapts immediately to NOT_FOUND or a cancelled status and stops before money is issued. A static plan must branch on those observations or replan; blindly following the remaining steps is unsafe. For this fixed refund workflow I would choose a validated conditional plan executed by deterministic Python rules, with human escalation above INR 1000. It reduces repeated model calls while retaining action-time checks. ReAct is preferable when policy or observations need more open-ended reasoning.
